home.heroTitle: Patient information on percutaneous hand surgery
home.heroPara1: Percutaneous hand surgery is a minimally invasive technique for treating common conditions such as carpal tunnel syndrome and trigger finger.
home.heroPara2: Using specialised Spirecut instruments and ultrasound guidance, surgeons can perform these procedures with high precision and safety — without any skin incision.
home.heroPara3: This website provides clear information about the procedures and helps patients prepare for the surgical and postoperative process.
home.whatPara1: The Spirecut procedure is a percutaneous (Latin: "through the skin") method. The entire intervention is performed through a needle puncture — it heals within one day, without any suture.
home.whatPara2: The procedure is performed under ultrasound guidance, similar to a pregnancy scan. This allows the surgeon to visualise nerves, blood vessels and ligaments in the hand far more clearly than in open surgery.
home.whatPara3: Spirecut instruments have a diameter of only 1.5 mm and are inserted through the needle puncture to release the constricting ligament.
advantages: No dressing or scar after the procedure
Specific instrument for two common hand conditions: carpal tunnel syndrome and trigger finger
home.quote: "Spirecut is a Swiss company that has developed instruments enabling ultrasound-guided procedures without a skin incision — based on the invention of Belgian surgeon Prof. Fabian Moungondo."
home.ctDesc: Tingling, numbness or pain in the fingers? The Spirecut Sono instrument gently and precisely releases the constricting transverse carpal ligament.
home.tfDesc: A finger that locks or snaps when bending? Spirecut's ring ligament release frees the tendon precisely under ultrasound — without a scalpel.

ct.heroTitle: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: Gentle Treatment Without Surgery
ct.heroDesc: Tingling fingers, night-time pain and numbness? The Spirecut® procedure offers a fast, minimally invasive solution.
ct.whatDesc: The carpal tunnel is a narrow channel at the wrist through which tendons and the median nerve pass. When the tissue in the carpal tunnel swells or the space becomes too tight, it compresses the nerve.
symptoms: Tingling in the thumb, index and middle finger
Pain that can radiate into the arm
ct.treatmentSubtitle: Why this new procedure is so beneficial for patients.
modernItems: Daily activities often possible the next day
ct.ctaTitle: Want to grip without pain again?
ct.ctaDesc: Get advice from a certified specialist on whether the Spirecut treatment is right for you.

tf.heroTitle: Trigger Finger: Release Without an Incision
tf.heroDesc: Your finger locks, snaps or hurts when bending? With Spirecut®, the constricting area is gently and precisely released — without conventional surgery.
tf.whatDesc: Trigger finger (also known as stenosing tenosynovitis) is caused by a thickening of the flexor tendon or the annular ligament. The tendon can no longer glide smoothly and catches. When trying to straighten the finger, the blockage often releases suddenly and with a jerk.
symptoms: Painful snapping when bending or straightening
A small, tender nodule at the palm
Morning stiffness in the affected finger
The finger remains stuck in a bent position
Pain at the base of the affected finger
tf.treatmentSubtitle: The modern, minimally invasive alternative to open hand surgery.
classicItems: Skin incision in the palm (annular ligament release)
Risk of painful scars on the gripping surface
modernItems: The finger is often freely movable right away
Just a plaster, no cumbersome dressing
tf.ctaTitle: Ready for a snap-free daily life?
tf.ctaDesc: The Spirecut procedure is performed on an outpatient basis and takes only a few minutes.

how.heroDesc: A medical breakthrough: safe, precise and entirely without an open skin incision, thanks to state-of-the-art ultrasound technology.

steps.title: Diagnosis and Consultation
steps.desc: First, the physician examines your hand with a high-resolution ultrasound device. The exact cause is determined and the procedure is discussed with you in detail.

steps.title: Local Anaesthesia
steps.desc: The procedure is performed on an outpatient basis. The relevant area of the hand is locally anaesthetised. You are awake but will feel no pain during the procedure.

steps.title: The Procedure Under Ultrasound
steps.desc: The fine Spirecut instrument is introduced through a tiny puncture site. The physician follows every step live on the ultrasound image. The constricting ligament is precisely released — surrounding tissue and nerves remain protected.

steps.title: After the Treatment
steps.desc: No suturing is required. The puncture site is simply covered with a small plaster. You can leave the practice shortly afterwards and often use your hand for everyday tasks the very next day.

praktisch.title: Practical Information
praktisch.intro: Your physician has scheduled an ultrasound-guided percutaneous procedure using the Spirecut method. We would like to explain how the procedure will proceed and what you can expect afterwards. Please note: depending on your individual situation, the organisation of the practice and your physician's experience, there may be minor or significant deviations from this general information. Always follow the recommendations and instructions of your treating physician.
praktisch.generalIntro: The procedure you will receive is percutaneous, ultrasound-guided and performed with the Spirecut technique. What do these terms mean?
praktisch.percutaneousDesc: The entire procedure is performed through a needle puncture that heals within one day after the operation. The puncture is comparable in size to an intravenous needle used for a blood draw. Therefore, the day after the procedure you do not require any further wound care — you can wash your hand and resume all normal activities. There are no sutures to remove.
praktisch.ultrasoundDesc: The procedure is performed under ultrasound guidance (the same device used to monitor foetal development during pregnancy, but with a different probe). This allows the surgeon to see nerves, blood vessels and ligaments in the hand often better than in a conventional open operation.
praktisch.spirecutDesc: Spirecut is a Swiss company that has developed instruments enabling ultrasound-guided procedures without a skin incision, based on the invention of Belgian surgeon Professor Fabian Moungondo. The Spirecut instruments are very fine (diameter: 1.5 mm) and are introduced through the needle puncture to release the ligament that is compressing your nerve or tendon.
praktisch.beforeIntro: Most procedures of this type do not require any specific preparation. Nevertheless, a few important points apply:
beforeItems: If you take blood thinners (e.g. Aspirin, Plavix, Xarelto, Eliquis, Pradaxa), inform your physician in advance. An adjustment may be required depending on the medication and dosage.
General anaesthesia is not required. You therefore do not need to fast, unless your physician explicitly instructs you to do so.
Plan to bring someone with you or take a taxi in case you feel unwell from the local anaesthesia.
praktisch.anaesthesiaDesc: The procedure is performed under local anaesthesia. Your physician injects an anaesthetic around the affected region. The injection itself may be briefly uncomfortable, but after a few minutes you should feel very little. You are awake during the procedure, but without pain in the hand.
praktisch.duringPara1: The surgeon introduces the Spirecut instrument through a needle puncture. Under continuous ultrasound guidance, the constricting ligament is precisely released. The procedure typically takes only a few minutes.
praktisch.duringPara2: Thanks to the ultrasound, the surgeon can ensure that all important structures (nerves, vessels) are protected. The risk of nerve injury is thus even lower than in open surgery.
afterItems: The puncture site is covered with a small plaster. You can leave the practice shortly after the procedure. Avoid wet hands and physical exertion in the first few hours.
The plaster can be removed. You can wash your hand and resume normal daily activities.
Some patients report mild pain in the first few days. Over-the-counter pain relievers (e.g. ibuprofen) can be taken as needed.
Your physician will tell you when and whether a follow-up appointment is required.
if you notice severe pain, swelling, fever or redness at the puncture site.

faq.heroDesc: Everything patients want to know before the procedure.
faq.notFoundDesc: A certified physician can answer all further questions about the method and your individual situation in a personal consultation.

items.a: No. The procedure is performed under local anaesthesia. You will feel no pain during the procedure, at most a slight pressure sensation. After the procedure, most patients report significantly less pain compared to open surgery.

items.q: How long does the procedure take?
items.a: The actual Spirecut procedure usually takes only a few minutes. Including preparation, ultrasound examination and anaesthesia, you should plan for a total visit of approximately 30 to 45 minutes.

items.q: When can I use my hand normally again?
items.a: Because no large incision is made and no sutures are needed, the hand heals significantly faster. Many patients can resume everyday activities (such as dressing or light office work) as early as the next day. However, you should avoid heavy physical strain for a few days.

Whether you need a referral depends on your health insurance and the specialist concerned. Most of the certified practices can be contacted directly. For private practices, a referral is generally not required.

items.q: Is Spirecut® covered by health insurance?
items.a: Spirecut is a highly advanced procedure and reimbursement can vary. Private health insurance typically covers the costs in full. For statutory insurance patients, it depends on the individual insurer and practice — it is often billed as a self-pay service (IGeL). Please ask the practice directly about the exact costs and reimbursement options.

As with any medical procedure, Spirecut carries risks such as minor bleeding or, in very rare cases, infection. Thanks to continuous ultrasound monitoring, the risk of injuring nerves or blood vessels is extremely low — even lower than in open surgery, since the physician can see the tissue live on the screen.

That is one of the greatest advantages: the instrument is so fine that only a small puncture like a needle mark is created (approx. 1 mm). There is no cutting and no suturing. Therefore, no visible or bothersome scar remains in the palm.
